Andres Iniesta rose from La Masia to win everything for club and country, and become one of the greatest midfielders of all time. In his own words, he tells FourFourTwo what it was like

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Leaving my family at 12 years old was one of the hardest things I’ve ever experienced. Above all, I felt fear. I was moving from my hometown, Fuentealbilla, not far from Valencia, and I was going to be alone in Barcelona. I was joining La Masia, but my first night there was tough for everyone, including my family. I couldn’t stop crying, and my father wanted to come and take me back home. Luckily, my mother changed his mind. We had to give it a try. I never thought about having to return to Fuentealbilla if I didn’t make it, nor did I obsess over how far I might go in football. What kept running through my mind was that I was at one of the best clubs in the world – I had to fulfil my dream of becoming a footballer.

I owe so much to my father – his advice, everything. He was my inspiration, and the one who pushed me to go to Barcelona in the first place. My essence as a footballer aligned with Barcelona’s style of play, so it was relatively easy to adapt when I started training at La Masia. I had to develop and perfect the concepts, but having the ball, positional play, working as a unit, that was the style I’d always had as a child in Albacete’s junior categories.

At Barcelona, I grew and gained experience – when I reached the youth team, that’s when I felt that the dream to become a footballer truly became mine. That’s when I thought, ‘This is serious now’. When I started playing for Barcelona B, I was one of those 17-year-old guys I used to look up to with excitement when I arrived at 12. That’s when I realised that it could be my time, but I always approached it with the intention of enjoying it – training with Rivaldo, Pep Guardiola, Phillip Cocu, Xavi and Carles Puyol, when I got the chance to join in with the first-team squad.

Michael Laudrup was my first big idol. I used to watch him closely and try to learn from his movements and elegance. I was also fascinated by Guardiola, not because he came from La Masia, but because of how he played. As a midfielder, I saw his vision of the game, how he positioned himself on the field, how he thought ahead of everyone else.

My connection with Xavi grew organically, without forcing anything. It grew over time, as we got more chances to play together. Maybe people forget now, but there was a time when it was said that we were incompatible. A lot was said, but we proved the opposite. We grew up with the same footballing philosophy and understood the game in the same way. When I was in the youth academy, Xavi had already heard about me, as he’s four years older than me. When I joined the first team, things gradually clicked until we eventually understood each other with just a glance.

The first time I joined up with the first team was special. I remember it with great emotion.

Carles Naval, Barça’s legendary team delegate, called La Masia to tell me that the manager Llorenc Serra Ferrer wanted me to start training with them. I didn’t know what to do at that moment. I was trembling all over. I went days without speaking. I’d spent years looking at Camp Nou from the window of La Masia. Now I was close to making my debut.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

After that, Louis van Gaal returned for a second spell as Barça’s coach. He was brave during a delicate time in Barça’s history. I remember we had a Under 19 European Championship with Spain, and he told me that he wanted me to start training permanently with the team during pre-season.

A year later, Ronaldinho arrived. He was different, groundbreaking – it was magical to watch him play, not just in matches, but also in training. He had spectacular physical power and technical quality far beyond any other player. He arrived at a challenging time for the club and brought back the fans’ hope and smiles. There’s a clear before and after in Barça’s modern history thanks to Ronaldinho.

We won La Liga after six years, then the Champions League in 2006, although I have bittersweet memories of that final against Arsenal in Paris. The priority was to win the Champions League, but being on the bench hurt that night because, in my view, it wasn’t fair – even if in football, the sense of fairness is very subjective.

When I found out that I wouldn’t be starting though, I didn’t let it bring me down. That’s never been my mentality. At that moment, all I thought about was being ready when Frank Rijkaard decided to bring me on, and to help win the trophy, which I did, when we came from a goal down to win.

We laid the foundations for a successful Barça. Ronaldinho paved the way for another genius: Messi. I cherish the small details of playing with him, the routine that never really felt like a routine, partly because of the way Leo surprised you every day. Training with him was incredible. We experienced amazing times on the pitch and many titles together, but I’ll always remember countless days at the training ground doing drills with incredible speed and precision. Tac, tac, tac. It was astonishing, and I feel privileged to have shared so many years with him.

In 2008, Guardiola became manager. From the very beginning, I had a feeling it was going to be a complete success. Personally, it was incredible to know that Guardiola was going to take charge of the team. Internally, I felt an immense sense of commitment and conviction, an indescribable motivation. Anyone who’s had the chance to work alongside one of their idols will understand me.

It was a great opportunity, and we realised it quickly. Pep was more than ready, and he conveyed that to the group during the first pre-season we had in Scotland. It was the conviction he had when explaining how he wanted us to play. He had everything planned out – from the defence, the positioning of the midfielders, to what the forwards had to do. You could see progress after just a few training sessions. The group executed Guardiola’s vision perfectly.

There was a lot of noise and doubt from the outside though, after we lost the first league game of the season to Numancia, then drew with Racing Santander at Camp Nou. One day, spontaneously, I decided to go to his office to reassure him. “Pep, don’t worry, everything will be fine,” I told him.

It wasn’t premeditated or discussed with the other captains. Maybe I decided to visit Guardiola because of the individual commitment I felt. I was convinced that great work was being done – we could sense it day by day and in the friendlies we played. We felt comfortable with that idea and were happy. What I conveyed to him was how the group felt. We were doing things right, and the momentum would change.

We won everything that season. But to win that Champions League final in Rome, we first had to get past Chelsea in the semi-finals. The second leg at Stamford Bridge will stay with me forever. Have I ever thought about what would have happened if I hadn’t scored in the 93rd minute? Never, just in case!

My shot was instinctive because I didn’t really have time to think about the execution. The ball came to me perfectly, and I knew roughly how I wanted to strike it. Luckily, it went to the one spot where Petr Cech couldn’t reach it, which was almost miraculous, considering he was as big as the goal itself. That ball was pushed in by all of us.

Winning that Champions League felt much better than three years earlier, even though I played injured in that final against Manchester United. I couldn’t shoot because of the risk of tearing a muscle, but internally I told myself: “I can’t miss this final after the one in Paris.” It turned out incredibly, although I paid the price afterwards with several muscle injuries.

A year before that, I’d also become a European champion with Spain. With the national team too, we had immense confidence in a specific playing style, and players who represented it perfectly. I credit the coach Luis Aragones for that. My best memory is when Iker Casillas lifted the European Championship trophy. So many generations had tried, and we managed to do it.

From the outside, a footballer’s life may seem perfect, particularly when you’re winning so many trophies. But we also have our worries. We’re human beings, too. I picked up several injuries after winning the Champions League final in Rome, and my great childhood friend Dani Jarque passed away. All of that made me hit rock bottom, but I tried not to give up, and I had the ability and humility to ask for professional help. I accepted that, at that moment, I was being consumed, that I needed other tools to get back on my feet. If I hadn’t done that, I imagine that my career would have been different. My family was also a great support.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, we lost our opening match. Afterwards, the message wasn’t exactly just ‘stay calm’, because when you lose your first game at a World Cup, the rest of the group stage is played under pressure. But we felt we’d played well against Switzerland. If we’d played that game 10 times, we would have won nine, so all we could do was keep trying, not doubt ourselves, and trust that we had the team to move forward. That’s what happened, and we progressed all the way to the final.

It was a tough and uncomfortable final. Rarely do those kinds of matches turn out to be open and entertaining. The Netherlands changed their style of play because of the opponent they were facing. They played aggressively, they showed us a lot of respect. The match was intense.

Then in extra time, I scored the winner. It’s hard to put that feeling into words. The ball came to me from Cesc Fabregas, I controlled it, and time stopped. It was like a slow-motion action. I heard silence. Why? I don’t know. I suppose the experience and responsibility from so many years at the elite level taught me to face high-pressure situations like that more calmly. Maybe someone else wouldn’t have even controlled the ball. That was the moment for Spain’s history to change with that World Cup.

During that era of Spanish football, maybe one of us could have won the Ballon d’Or, but it’s not something I dwell on. Whoever wins it deserves to, especially if it was Messi. I’ve had the chance to attend many of those ceremonies, and of course, anyone would love to win it, but it’s not something that bothers me at all. The image of Xavi, Messi and me – three guys from La Masia – on the podium in 2010 was bigger than winning it. That was the real prize.

In 2011, we won another Champions League together, this time at Wembley, against Manchester United again. Wembley is a sacred place for Barcelona fans – it was where the club became European champions for the first time, in 1992.

Facing Manchester United gave even more weight to that final. I remember preparing for it in great detail. We’d just won La Liga, and had two weeks to focus on that night. We travelled to England earlier than usual. We knew how Manchester United played, how to exploit their weaknesses and we had everything memorised. We went into half-time drawing 1-1, but we felt completely in control. We were dominating, and everything was unfolding as we wanted. It was perfect, and eventually we won 3-1.

We won a lot during that era under Guardiola, even though in life you lose more than you win. In fact, I don’t even remember exactly how many titles we lifted. Looking back now, I realise how much effort it all took. Behind it all was a group of players with hunger and excitement, whose every victory motivated us to stay at the top. Maybe back then we didn’t value a Spanish Super Cup or a Copa del Rey as much as we should have done, but you have to celebrate and savour everything. It all matters. Fans eagerly awaited our matches to see us play, and that says it all.

Despite the exceptional and privileged life of being a professional footballer and playing for Barça though, I never felt different from others – or at least, I tried to live my life that way. From the outside, it might seem difficult to understand, but for me, it wasn’t hard to remain Andres. The closer you stay to the reality around you, the better. I know we’re sometimes seen as unapproachable, but I’ve always tried to be a normal person.

If you’re at Barça, there’s no better place to be. Since leaving my hometown of Fuentealbilla, I was convinced that it was the club where I wanted to stay. It became my home. My goal was always to succeed there and stay as long as possible, so in that sense, I was never tempted by the Premier League.

Early in my career, I’m told there was some talk about Rangers trying to sign me on loan, but I don’t remember it clearly. I’m not sure if they ever directly contacted my father or my agent. In any case, what I can say is that I never seriously considered leaving the club. Not at the beginning, nor later. I always had confidence that I would succeed at Barça and never entertained the idea of going on loan. I told myself, ‘Even if I don’t play much, I’m convinced I’ll end up playing’. A few minutes at Barça were worth more than anywhere else.

I would have liked to retire at Barça, but I had to make other decisions, and I think I did so at the right time, when I signed for Vissel Kobe in 2018. My last final for Barça, the Copa del Rey final against Sevilla, was unforgettable. I felt like I was flying on the pitch, everything just flowed, and I could end that wonderful chapter with a goal I’ll never forget. We won 5-0 – it was unbelievable!

Leaving wasn’t easy, but the club demands 300 per cent, and I couldn’t give that any more. Could I have stayed another year? Maybe, but I left with the memory of Iniesta as a Barça player in an incredible moment.

A few months ago, I announced my retirement at the age of 40, after a year playing for Emirates Club in the UAE Pro League. Which word defines how I feel about my career? Pride, in having worked hard until the very last training session. The rest is history: titles, defeats, good moments and bad ones. But what stands out to me is never giving up. I would have played until I was 90, but I’m happy to have fulfilled the dream of becoming a footballer.

For now, I plan to definitely stay in Dubai for 2025, then we’ll see. There’s family logistics to consider, like our children’s education, so we’ll try to manage it all. I’m also working on projects that allow me to keep learning. I don’t have time to get bored, even though everything is different. I still have the passion and enthusiasm to do what I do with commitment and dedication.

I’m doing a bit of everything – this is a new chapter of my life where I want to grow and explore different things. I have several businesses, like my agency Never Say Never (NSN) or Mikakus Barcelona, a sneaker company. I’m pursuing new interests with my team and we’ve invested in an exciting project at the Danish club Helsingor. I’ll try to absorb as much knowledge as possible over the coming months. I’m also enthusiastic about studying for my coaching licence in the future. Coaching motivates me a lot.

I know that many people expect me to coach Barça one day, but right now, I’m not thinking about that. For me, that’s a huge responsibility, especially since I’m just starting out. Of course it’s my home though, and hopefully one day I’ll return – we’ll see in what capacity and when. It would be beautiful. Guardiola, Xavi, and then Iniesta? Sounds good…

#1069. Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals

Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.

They are the two players who have defined the last two decades. As football became ever more popular, commercial and dominant in the cultural and sporting landscape, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi remained its twin peaks.

Along with that has come endless social media posts, stories and discussions about who is better. Does Messi's World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina trump Ronaldo's Euro 2016 win and two Nations League titles? Or does the Portuguese's greater number of goals mean more? How about their club honors?

It is, essentially, a subjective argument and not one that can ever be resolved. It remains to be seen whether that's also true of the public spat between Ronaldo and his Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

On Tuesday, Messi scored a 126th goal in his 208th game for Argentina. Shortly before he did, Ronaldo posted a 2,000-word statement in which he stopped short of quitting the national team but said there was an "absolute breakdown of trust" between him and the coach.

Ronaldo's comments refer to Portugal's recent match against Norway in which he said he was initially to be rested before being asked to warm up as a substitute without ever being brought on. The striker, 41, walked away from the team's camp for the remainder of the international break, but said the story is not over.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," said Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

"Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach's word, as anyone who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it," Ronaldo said. "The responsibility is entirely mine. I apologize to the Portuguese people once again, but the breaking of one's word has, for me, a defining impact.

"I felt that, from that point on, my staying would only harm the group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left," he continued before suggesting he accepted there may be a need for the coach or federation to punish him.

It was a long way from the emotional scenes in Rosario, Argentina. Instead of anger and recrimination, the overriding emotions there were gratitude, nostalgia and sadness.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you," Messi, who now plays his club football for Inter Miami in the US, told the 80,000 fans who had packed in to see him score a penalty in a 3-0 win over Benin.

For some, the contrasting evenings offered a neat synopsis of the pair. Ronaldo, less naturally gifted than his counterpart, has made the most of his talents with a singular focus which many believe often makes him prioritize himself over the team. He has had similar fallouts with managers and head coaches before, including Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Erik ten Hag at Manchester United and Portugal's 2022 World Cup coach, Fernando Santos.

Ronaldo's much-discussed aim to reach 1,000 career goals is held up by some as further evidence of where his motivations lie.

"You know what my goal is. I want to win trophies, and I want to reach that number (1,000 goals) that you all know. I will reach the number for sure, if no injuries," he said last December. He is currently on 979.

For others, that is simply what is required to be the best. While Messi's quiet character and general refusal to play out his life in public suggest a more humble character focused on helping the team, his genius has undoubtedly changed the teams around him. In the 2026 World Cup, he barely broke into a run but still led an otherwise fairly limited Argentina to the final with eight goals.

There will be no more Messi goals for Argentina and, despite his promises, no absolute assurances that the world will see Ronaldo in a Portugal shirt again. For now, both will head back to their club sides to play out their twilight years away from the intensity of Europe's top leagues. But wherever they go from here, the spotlight will keep following.

#1068. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1067. The ‘magical night’ Man United must replicate to halt slide into chaos

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

With a fractured dressing room and fans in open revolt, the beleaguered head coach needs a result against Roma akin to their 2007 triumph to arrest the club’s decline

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

When the Champions League draw pitted Manchester United against Roma, the more nostalgic were transported back 20 seasons. To a night that, ultimately, proved a staging post on Sir Alex Ferguson’s way to conquering Europe the following season. To a European Cup win that, in its margin, has only been bettered in United’s history by the Busby Babes’ 10-0 demolition of Anderlecht in 1956. To the only time in 464 appearances for United that Michael Carrick scored twice.

In 2007, United faced a Roma side that included the World Cup winners Francesco Totti and Daniele de Rossi. They thrashed them 7-1. “A magical night,” Carrick recalled. “It was one of the best nights, one of the best games, one of the best atmospheres I've been fortunate enough to witness. So the fact that I scored a couple and that was very unusual gives me great, great memories, but it was more the actual whole the emotion of the night. It was a special one.”

But Carrick’s initial response had been: “Long time ago, hey?” Increasingly, that comment could be applied to many of the good times: to the heady days in spring when he won 12 of his first 17 games after returning to Old Trafford. Now, nine without a win, beaten in each of the last three, Carrick could do with recapturing some of the magic he and his teammates produced to inflict Roma’s record European defeat. Although, as Gian Piero Gasperini’s team are third in Serie A and, two weeks ago, United lost 4-1 to the side now fourth in the Italian top flight, it feels unlikely. But, almost two decades ago, United had lost consecutive games before welcoming Roma to Old Trafford. Things can change, quickly and dramatically.

“You might think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on, but I genuinely, really can't wait for the game,” said Carrick. And indeed, it may sound delusional; or, at the least, the words of a man who remembers what United was and imagines it could be again.

But not, perhaps, with him as manager, or this group of players, or this hierarchy or these owners. Carrick’s cryptic reference to “what’s going on” was shorthand for the public criticisms of either him or Jason Wilcox voiced by Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez, of the Argentinian’s sending-off at Chelsea, of the fans’ audible dissent against the sporting director, the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, of the possibility this is his last week in the job.

“I can’t look into the future,” said Carrick. “You never know what's going to happen.” Lose to Roma and then Aston Villa and his position would seem untenable; but then it did when United were beaten by Bournemouth last Sunday and he was given a stay of execution.

But too few of Carrick’s squad seem intent on keeping him. The feckless Martinez, whose recklessness ensured defeat on Sunday, is a case in point and, after a series of wretched performances, Carrick faces a decision whether to select the Argentinian. It is his way to defend his players and he said: “I've got no concerns about [his] commitment at all. The dressing room is a good, good place, so perceptions are a funny thing.”

The loyalists, the men still in Carrick’s camp, definitely include Kobbie Mainoo, who has known the older midfielder he was 14 and the former United captain was beginning his coaching career. Carrick revived Mainoo’s fortunes, after Ruben Amorim had marginalised him, when he took temporary charge in January. “I’m grateful for the trust the boss has put in me,” he said. “Knowing he's a player who's been at this club and knows the history of this club and knows what it takes to win, I take those words to heart.”

It may be a rare speck of good news for Carrick that Mainoo returned from injury as a substitute at Chelsea. United have only lost one game the Mancunian has started this season.

Mainoo said the players appreciate Carrick’s tactic of trying to shield them from criticism. He knows that they owe him. “Of course,” he said. “And I feel like our way to repay that is to be behind the manager on the pitch and off it, and fight for us and fight for us as a team.”

The supporters have made it clear where their allegiances lie, serenading Carrick and booing the players after Bournemouth’s emphatic win, and Mainoo reflected: “In these tough times you can't expect the fans 100,000 percent of the time to be to be happy and cheering when we're not putting out results.”

Which they have not been. There could be consequences, and not merely for Carrick. The 2008 Champions League winner played in three finals of this competition. Now United have lost their last two European matches and their next five – Roma, Sporting CP, Leipzig, Bayern Munich and Villarreal – offer few guarantees of victory for a stumbling side. United risk becoming the first Premier League club to fail to even get a top-24 finish in this revamped format. “There is the bigger picture and it is about getting through to the later stages,” said Carrick.

As he knows, United once surged into a Champions League semi-final with a 7-1 demolition. But that was a long time ago.

#1066. Patrick Stewart dies: how Captain Picard inspired today’s science leaders

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Actor Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard.Credit: RGR Collection/Alamy

Researchers have joined the chorus of Star Trek fans expressing grief at the death of actor Patrick Stewart, who played the legendary Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

Stewart, who died on 28 October aged 86, portrayed Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation from 1987 to 1994 and in various films from the franchise. As captain of the starship USS Enterprise, Picard led his crew on galactic explorations in the twenty-fourth century, where they encountered new worlds and civilizations. For many scientists, Captain Picard exemplified the qualities of a good scientific leader.

“His first immediate thought was to consider all angles and to ask questions,” says Sarah Bickerton, a public-policy researcher at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. But more importantly, says Bickerton, Picard consulted his Enterprise crew members — irrespective of rank — before making decisions. That shaped Bickerton’s own leadership approach. She says she makes a point of consulting her research assistants and graduate students on important decisions.

A film from the franchise that had an impact on Bickerton was Star Trek: First Contact (1996), in which Picard travels back in time to the twenty-first century and explains that in the future, money does not exist. “We work to better ourselves and the rest of humanity,” Picard says.

Bickerton says: “For scientists, that really resonates. What drives us is bettering ourselves and the rest of humanity through the search for knowledge and just to learn and understand.”

Other researchers have also been inspired by Picard’s style of leadership. In a 2025 interview with Kentucky Alumni magazine, Tracy Drain, a flight systems engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, said that she loved how the character modelled what an excellent leader could be. “He was even-keeled, respectful, kind to everyone,” she said. “He encouraged his crew to think outside the box and supported them in what they needed to do.”

On social media, scientists expressed how the character of Picard influenced their scientific careers.

Jordan Harrison, a psychologist in Ann Arbor, Michigan, wrote on Bluesky: “I can trace my initial interest in science, my love of space and astronomy, the seeds of an ethic of care for others different than me, and early memories of bonding with my dad over pop culture to Star Trek: TNG and Patrick Stewart’s portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard. This one hurts.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03543-9

The Danish legend missed out on his country's only major tournament victory

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 30 years on, Denmark's Euro 92 victory remains one of international football's most remarkable stories.

A team that had failed to qualify for the tournament would eventually go on to lift the trophy, having taken full advantage of Yugoslavia's ejection following the break-up of the country.

Goals from John Jensen and Kim Vilfort sealed a 2-0 win over Germany in the final, with the Danes claiming the stunning victory without one of their greatest-ever players, following Michael Laudrup's decision to walk away from international football two years earlier to focus on his Barcelona career.

The mercurial midfielder had been central to the rise of Danish Dynamite, the thrilling side that reached the semi-finals of Euro 84 before winning over the hearts and minds of so many at the 1986 World Cup. But his decision to prioritise club football meant he would miss Denmark's greatest triumph.

Speaking about the Danish side of the 1980s, Laudrup credited his manager and his team-mates' decision to ply their trade in Europe's best leagues.

"A lot of the players were playing for big clubs in Europe, at a time when not many foreign players were allowed in European leagues," Laudrup tells FourFourTwo. "We had a lot of individual quality. The arrival of Sepp Piontek as manager in 1979 was also pivotal – he fulfilled our potential. We went to the European Championship and beat Yugoslavia 5-0. We had a fantastic game against Belgium too, which we won 3-2 from 2-0 down. In the end, we only lost on penalties in the semi-final against Spain.

"At the 1986 World Cup, we beat Uruguay 6-1 and West Germany 2-0, but then went out against Spain in the last 16. We were 1-0 up, but a poor second half cost us and we lost 5-1. The big countries had tournament experience. We learned from that and could apply it in 1992 and 1998, where we achieved good results in the latter stages."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

And what about his decision to quit the Denmark team in 1990?

"In the second game of qualifying, we drew in Northern Ireland, then we lost at home against Yugoslavia, who had a fantastic team," Laudrup continues. "I realised they’d qualify, even if we beat them away. I was also in the early stages of my time at Barça, which was important to me, and the two teams played completely different football. I wasn’t really happy with the way we played in the national team, but it’s always the manager’s decision. Still, I thought, ‘With this style of play, I can never be the same as at Barcelona.’

"As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. People asked me if I wanted to go, but I didn’t want to join at the last moment, even though I could have. I felt it wouldn’t have been fair."

Laudrup would eventually return to the Danish national side in 1993.

"I’d won three league titles and the European Cup with Barça, and every time, they asked if I wanted to go back," he explains. "I’d achieved all the things I wanted with Barcelona, so I agreed. Unfortunately we lost a World Cup qualifier to Spain – the third time they got in our way, after beating us in 1984 and 1986. Spain has given me so much at personal and club level, then it’s curious how much it has taken away from me with the national team! But then we went to Euro 96 and the 1998 World Cup."

His 100th international cap came during the 1998 World Cup, with Laudrup calling time on his international career following their quarter-final defeat to Brazil.

"That was a great stage to retire on," he reflects. "After leaving Real Madrid, I went to Japan – I wanted to go somewhere I could still play, but also have a bit of freedom after being in Southern Europe since 1983. I thought maybe I should retire from the national team, but the coach asked me to continue. I realised that even though I liked life in Japan, I wanted to finish at a higher level. There was some interest from countries like Turkey and France – Marseille wanted me – but the Southern European passion was what I didn’t want any more! [Laughs]

"I joined Ajax – that team was incredible, with the De Boer brothers, Danny Blind, Edwin van der Sar and Jari Litmanen. We won the Double, so I continued with the national team, we qualified for the World Cup and lost in the quarter-finals to Brazil. We really challenged them and it was a great way to finish my career."

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1064. Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease

After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.

UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.

Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.

She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."

All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.

The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.

Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.

A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.

Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.

Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.

The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

#1063. The baffling question surrounding Unai Emery and Aston Villa ahead of Barcelona showdown

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Emery has worked wonders at Villa Park, with a Champions League trip to Camp Nou the latest reward, but where his managerial future lies continues to be a topic of debate

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It is the biggest club from England’s second city against the biggest from Spain’s. And if the similarities between Birmingham and Barcelona may end there – the Brummie separatist movement is rather less prominent that its Catalan counterpart, for instance – then a trip to Camp Nou is both a sign of a new eminence and part of a broader question about Aston Villa’s status.

In footballing terms, England’s second city has often tended to be Manchester, Liverpool or London. The notion that Villa will forever lie further down the footballing food chain seemed to underpin Jamie Carragher’s somewhat derogatory comments last week; even if Villa’s threat to sue the pundit, signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris, struck many as frankly silly.

Meanwhile, Unai Emery wore his Villa blazer to the Ballon d’Or ceremony last week. It could be interpreted as a gesture of his enduring loyalty, amid the possibility the Manchester United job will become vacant; but perhaps he simply liked the garment.

Whichever, Villa may have one of the two finest managers currently working in the Premier League, along with Emery’s fellow Basque Mikel Arteta, and one of the best in Europe; his record five Europa League wins indicates as much. Villa’s renaissance has been inspired by Emery and can feel reliant upon him.

They could be a club who are establishing themselves as a regular presence on such nights or one who may not been seen again at Camp Nou for decades; in March, Newcastle, like Villa now, in a second Champions League campaign in three seasons, lost 7-2 to Barcelona. It remains to be seen if they will return any time soon.

For Villa, this is a first game against Barcelona at their iconic stadium for 43 years, since a Super Cup defeat; Villa were European champions then and won the second leg 3-0. It was their last continental trophy until Emery’s side beat Freiburg in May.

Villa are ticking off the clashes with the European superpowers. Two years ago, they renewed acquaintances with Bayern Munich and, as they did in the 1982 European Cup final, beat them 1-0. They ran Paris Saint-Germain close in the 2025 quarter-finals, only narrowly lost to them in this summer’s Super Cup and face them again next month. It only really leaves Real Madrid of the current elite to face.

For Emery, a return to his native Spain can serve as a reminder that he has never been hired by any of their three major forces. Atletico Madrid can at least offer the reason that Diego Simeone has been in situ for 15 years. Real may feel that Emery’s obsessive attention to detail may not be suited to their superstars or that his relative lack of charisma may not work at the Bernabeu. Barcelona tend to look for managers who fit into their traditions and suit their tactics. Emery’s sides are often entertaining, but he did not study at the school of tiki-taka.

Instead, he punched above his weight with other clubs in his homeland. He finished third in LaLiga three times with Valencia, won a hat-trick of Europa Leagues with Sevilla and a fourth with Villarreal.

He became the master of knockout competitions; indeed Emery has won three Europa Leagues since Barcelona last won the Champions League. And yet a competition Villa were knocked out of showed their priorities in their new reality. A heavily weakened side exited the Carabao Cup at Bournemouth last week; Emery has his sights on grander targets. After three straight wins, Villa could be on course for another top-eight group-stage finish in the Champions League.

Meanwhile, as the ‘big six’ looks an increasingly anachronistic term, the changing landscape of English football offers the chance for Villa to be frequent top-five finishers in the immediate future. Remarkably, the last English club outside the supposedly big six to play in the European Cup or Champions League, excluding qualifiers, in consecutive seasons is Villa themselves: between 1981 and 1983, entering the competition in the second season as holders.

So Emery’s reign could assume historic proportions, and not merely at Villa Park. And in that respect, one of the biggest games in Villa’s history may only be the second largest of their week.

Their trip to Old Trafford on Sunday may be framed by the discussions about Michael Carrick, his possible successors, arguably the best qualified of all, in Emery, and perhaps the favourite, in Eddie Howe. Whereas Howe concluded he could not develop a second terrific team with Newcastle, there are encouraging signs that Emery can with Villa. If he has a decision to make, that might shape it.

And a comparison of Villa and United now, whether in terms of the starting 11s, the direction of travel, the Premier League table or the Champions League table, could show a shift in the balance of power. Villa certainly looks the more appealing prospect. But for some, the question may be not why he does not go to United, but why Spain’s big three don’t come in for him.

The former Liverpool defender has been a Sky Sports regular for more than a decade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Immediately after hanging up his boots, Jamie Carragher moved into the media world, with Sky Sports signing up the former Liverpool and England defender at the start of the 2013/14 season.

Over the past 13 years, Carragher has become of the most recognisable and distinct voices in football broadcasting, whether that was sparring with Gary Neville on Monday Night Football back in the day, or showing his lighter side on shows such as Stick to Football.

But how does he assess his own evolution from player to pundit? And how does he compare himself with his former on-pitch rival Neville?

“There are parts of understanding football where Gary’s on a completely different level to me – his understanding of how the leagues work, or the EFL,” Carragher tells FourFourTwo, referencing Neville’s role as co-owner of League Two club Salford City.

“He’s in meetings because he’s an owner, and he had a really good take on things like Covid, when there was no football going on, and also things like a football regulator and how deals are done, whereas I don’t. He’s an authority on subjects like that. And he’s also the authority on winning the Premier League – I have to accept that.”

For Carragher, research, preparation and tactical insight is where he excels in front of camera – even if on a show such as Stick to Football, that can get overshadowed by a witty one-liner from someone else on the panel. “It can be a little frustrating,” Carragher smiles.

“But that’s the nature of the show. If I make a point, then someone comes out with, ‘It’s just 11 vs 11, it’s just 22 men kicking the ball around’, you can think, ‘What’s f**king the point in anything!’”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For Carragher, though, it’s this detail and alternative ways of analysing the game that keeps him engaged.

“But everybody sees the game in a different way, and I love the details – that’s what gets my juices flowing,” he continues. “Finding something or a bit of analysis that no one else has seen.

“A lot of the time there are these myths in football, about things that happened years ago, but when you actually look at the detail, they didn’t f**king happen!”

Given his love for detail, how does Carragher view this stage of his career in football, compared to his playing days? “I was a very good player, but I’m a great pundit,” he jokes.

“Modest!” laughs Neville, sat beside him. “As for me, I always said that on my tombstone, it would say ‘Six out of 10’. I like the idea of being consistent.

“I don’t think I’m better as a pundit or player, I think I’m consistent.”

#1061. David Moyes salutes Everton after successive wins against Newcastle

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Toffees backed up their 3-1 Carabao Cup victory last Thursday with a 1-0 success at St James’ Park

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

David Moyes hailed a “great result” for Everton as they secured back-to-back wins over Newcastle with a 1-0 triumph at St James’ Park.

Monday night’s Premier League clash took place just four days after the Toffees claimed a 3-1 victory over the Magpies in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup and Moyes’ side were able to secure three points on Tyneside.

A first half lacking in clear-cut chances from both sides saw Everton take the lead just four minutes after the restart when Tyrique George’s low effort squeezed underneath Lukas Hornicek.

Thierno Barry then reacted quickly to pounce on the loose ball and stab home for his fourth league goal of the campaign.

Moyes admitted recording successive wins over the Magpies in such a short space of time was “not an easy thing”, but was full of praise for his side’s display as they claimed three points.

“They are so good in what they do as they give everything they’ve got,” the Everton boss said.

“They’re a brilliant group of players and they’ve had it tough as well. They want to keep winning and they’ve found it difficult with the way things have gone, but they’re pulling it out and doing their best to be in all the games.

“It’s never easy… we beat Newcastle on Thursday night and to beat them again today is not an easy thing to do for any club and this level.

“To come here and get a good win tonight was a great result for us.”

Victory ends a three-game winless run for Everton in the Premier League and sees them move into seventh in the standings, but Moyes was also pleased to earn a first away win in their league campaign.

He added: “We’ve actually done quite well in some of the games getting draws in difficult away games, but we’ve not picked up a victory and last season we had a great run of results away from home.

“So I was hoping to pick it up tonight and thankfully we did, clean sheet and got the goal that counted.”

Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle admitted his side need to “do things better” following a disappointing performance.

The Magpies struggled to threaten throughout the match and were frustrated further when Jacob Ramsey was dismissed with two yellow cards in quick succession at the death to leave the Tynesiders 13th in the table.

Asked what the solution is, Jaissle said: “We need to analyse that now in detail.

“It’s also clear that I have the responsibility and I also take that as the manager of this club, and we need to do things better.

“There were many things there, not only in possession, which was not on the level we expected to see.

“Also out of possession, we wanted to press them high, we wanted to stretch them as soon as possible and make also a clear distinction if that was overplayed from their position that we defend in a compact block, but nothing between.

“Again, it was not much seen today on the pitch.”

#1060. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

After that? Liverpool swarmed over Arsenal, particularly in the first-half with Florian Wirtz’s free-kick cannoning back off the crossbar and Mac Allister somehow heading over. He was six yards out and unmarked, it was a glorious chance.

That was the hosts’ last tangible opportunity to score. As well as Arsenal defended, it was not a good afternoon for Liverpool’s forwards, Bradley Barcola in particular, although it was interesting to see Arsenal double-up on Rio Ngumoha when he came on. Arteta reacted by bringing on a second left-back, in Piero Hincapié.

Arsenal had the best chance with Alisson denying Christos Tzolis as the Greek winger’s low volley threatened to arc around him.

For Liverpool it became frantic. They could not surf the emotion, not against this battle-hardened Arsenal.

Boos rang out at the end – signs of how Arsenal had frustrated Liverpool – as Arteta gained his first win at Anfield as a manager. He was in the last Arsenal team to win here as a player 14 years ago. But this one meant more – that was also clear and obvious as he joyfully jumped into the arms of his assistant, Gabriel Heinze.

It’s not about me [being brave in picking Nyoni], it’s about Trey. In training he has shown he has the level. For us he’s very good without the ball. It’s a big challenge for him but [he is ready].

He is young but covers a lot of space. He is aggressive as well without the ball, calm in possession, good communicating with his team-mates which is good when you know how Arsenal play. You need a lot of change of marks [positions]. There have to be a lot of things done there in the middle and he has done that in other games.

The aggression we had [against Brighton, never resting] in their structures, we go again, recover, go vertical, attack the spaces in behind, win the chance battle, one v one situations. Don’t concede territory against teams like Brighton and Arsenal. We have to be as aggressive as we were in that match.

Teams like this don’t give you easy situations [to score]. We have to be good in one v one, shots from outside the box, finishes, set plays – we should be a team that is strong in set plays. You won’t get many chances against Arsenal and when you have one you’ve got to grab it.

Yes we had good results with Bournemouth against Arsenal but the strengths of my team in Liverpool are different so you have to approach it in a different way. There are things I can use [from Bournemouth] but not a lot.

Arsenal have lost three of their last four games against Bournemouth when Iraola was in charge.

We have been very close [to winning at Anfield in the last four seasons] but moments have decided those games. We have to be really precise in those moments for victory here and that has to be the case today.

Every manager has different solutions and a different approach and Andoni’s is very clear. We expect a different game to that one [last year when Arne Slot’s side won 1-0]. It is a team that is very vertical with a real capacity to create chaos from almost all situations. They’re very good in the high press with great individuals.

[On selection] We have had issues this week with ankles and other things and had to be smart how we manage the minutes today to have players for the minutes they are available for. The conditions and the context force you to make certain decisions [on Tzolis coming straight back in after a month out].

We can’t wait. This is the kind of opportunity, challenge, mission you want to come to Anfield for.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. In his pre-match press conference Arteta noted concerns about Noni Madueke (ankle), Declan Rice (thigh). Riccardo Calafiori (unspecified) and Christos Tzolis who has returned to training but all are expected to be available. Andoni Iraola has ruled out Jeremie Frimpong as well as long-term casualties Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley but hopes to be able to include Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz. Team news should come through at 3.15pm

#1059. Nobel Prize in chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.

The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.

Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.

The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."

The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

#1057. Asian Cup postponed following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

The 24-team tournament was due to kick off in January but has been moved back to at least December 2027

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The 2027 Asian Cup has been postponed by almost up to a year following recent attacks on hosts Saudi Arabia, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has confirmed.

The tournament, which was due to kick-off on January 7, has been rescheduled due to “exceptional circumstances”, the AFC said.

In October, a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claiming responsibility.

The AFC said the 24-team tournament could now take place from December 23 next year to January 21, 2028.

"The new dates of the tournament will be presented to Fifa for approval," the AFC said.

“Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

Several Premier League players, including Aston Villa’s Japan international goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, Manchester City’s Uzbekistan international defender Abdukodir Khusanov and Hull City’s Australia international defender Lucas Herrington, would have had to leave their clubs mid-season to take part in the tournament but will now be available for their teams this season.

Disruptions in travel and security concerns have affected other sporting events in Saudi Arabia, ‌with the Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December. Not all sport in the region ‌has been called off, however, with Saul "Canelo" ​Alvarez beating Christian Mbilli in their world title bout in Riyadh on Saturday.

The former USMNT international was heralded as the game’s next superstar when he was coming up through the ranks

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freddy Adu was barely into his teenage years when the hype began.

Even before he made his senior debut at D.C. United as a 14-year-old, Adu was heralded as ‘the next Pele’ as he was talked up as not just a promising young player, but a generational talent who was being tipped for global stardom.

But compared to the Brazilian great at such a young age came with a weight of expectation that no child should have to even comprehend, let alone live up to. As Adu looks back at this career, he explains that the excitement of being compared to his idol would soon give way to the realisation that he needed to forge his own path.

Asked by FourFourTwo when he realised he might be destined for something special, Adu says: “When I was 11 or 12. My team, the Bethesda Internationals, were one of the top four teams in the nation and we were in the national championships.

“A lot of teams were playing, there were a bunch of fields, and when my team played, everybody – and I mean everybody, all the other parents, all the other teams – would come and gather around our field to watch.”

This was the first time that Adu had experienced this kind of attention, as his matches became must-watch affairs for local fans and players.

“They’d heard of this 11-year-old, and it was under 14s, so I was playing three years up. It was really cool – that was the first time I got a taste of pressure,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

This excitement would grow, with Adu’s name going way past youth tournaments and into the mainstream media.

As a consequence of this, comparisons with Pele, Adu’s hero, began to emerge.

“As a kid, when I first heard it, I thought it was cool to be compared to your idol, because Pele was my idol,” Adu continues.

But eventually, the enormity of the situation would sink in and the comparison to the three-time World Cup winner and all-time great began to weigh on him.

“Then it set in that ‘Oh my God…’ It took a few months to realise ‘Alright, now you’ve really got to perform’, because people aren’t just comparing anybody to Pele. Then I started thinking ‘You can’t allow this to happen’.

“I had to say ‘Look, I’m my own player, you can’t compare me to one of the greatest players who ever played, I’m not him’. I had to come to terms with being my own player and just focus on being me, rather than being Pele.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. It's going to be bumpy, but certain numbers suggest he deserves time to implement his tactics at Newcastle.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Replacing a club legend is never easy, especially when overseeing a major squad rebuild. But despite losing key figures like Bruno Guimarães, Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Kieran Trippier, Matthias Jaissle has guided Newcastle United to eighth in the Premier League, two points behind fifth-placed Chelsea.

For a club that has played Champions League football in two of the last three seasons, expectations remain considerably higher. Newcastle's inconsistent results have raised questions about their progress under Jaissle, but beneath the surface, there are promising signs that the German is laying the bedrock for a new era.

Newcastle recorded the Premier League's sixth-best expected goals against (50.95) but conceded 55 goals last season, the sixth-worst tally in the division, and finished 12th. Jaissle initially struggled to address those weaknesses, conceding eight goals in his first four league matches and two against West Bromwich Albion in the EFL Cup.

However, the underlying numbers suggest a marked improvement. According to Gradient Sports, Newcastle ranked 19th in the Premier League for tackling and duel performance across the opening four weeks of the season. Over the next four weeks, they climbed to seventh and sixth, respectively, while their positioning ranking jumped from 13th to third.

Newcastle's center backs rose from 16th to eighth in average overall performance grade, their fullbacks from fourth to first, and their aerial duels from eighth to first. These upgrades suggest a more cohesive defensive unit, but individual shortcomings remain a concern: Sven Botman has committed a league-high five errors leading to shots this season.

"We are searching now for stabilisation" Matthias Jaissle speaks ahead of Newcastle's visit to Everton in the Carabao Cup! 🎙️ https://t.co/jNZtpCJ4MFOctober 29, 2026

There has been progress in midfield, too. With Guimarães and Tonali gone, Lewis Miley has assumed greater responsibility, improving his average grade by 11.15 points between the opening four weeks and the following four. Nico González's grade has also increased by 9.20 points over the same period.

But while Jaissle has improved the team's defense and midfield, attack is another story. Newcastle's wingers have dropped from ninth to 18th in average performance between the two four-week periods, while their center forwards climbed from 19th to 18th. Newcastle also rank 16th for expected goals per match and chance quality, and joint 13th for shots.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The successive departures of Alexander Isak and Gordon have deprived Newcastle of two major attacking weapons, and their replacements have struggled to fill the void. Jaissle has fortified their defensive base, but he has yet to develop an attacking structure capable of creating gilt-edged chances, and he is yet to find his strongest team.

Nevertheless, last weekend's trip to Crystal Palace offered plenty of reason for optimism. After three defeats in four matches, Jaissle made five changes to his starting XI, replacing Botman and Malick Thiaw with Dan Burn and Fabian Schär, while restoring Amar Dedić, Jacob Murphy and William Osula to the lineup.

These changes paid dividends. Burn and Schär helped the Magpies secure their first clean sheet in two months, while Murphy and Dedić assisted goals for Osula and Harvey Barnes. And instead of dropping between the center backs, González operated further forward and was more involved in Newcastle's attacking buildup.

After a subdued first half, Newcastle showed more urgency in exploiting turnovers and scored twice in the first 13 minutes after the restart. It offered a glimpse of what they could look like if Jaissle can fix an attack that has been declining since Eddie Howe's last year in charge. However, Thursday's defeat to Everton served as a reminder of the inconsistency that continues to plague their growth.

Unlike at Red Bull Salzburg and Al-Ahli, where he enjoyed substantial financial backing and squads capable of competing for silverware, Jaissle is now overseeing a Newcastle team in transition. With several established starters gone and their replacements still finding their feet, this is undoubtedly a work in progress.

It would be premature to call the Palace victory a turning point, but the data suggests that Jaissle is gradually building a stronger foundation. Whether they can translate that progress into a sustained push for European qualification will depend on solving the problem that has persisted throughout his tenure: making Newcastle lethal in the final third.

From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing.
